definition: Grandiose means grand in an inflated way that outruns real substance, sense, or means.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word grandiose. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know grandiose should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The garage band's plans were grandiose from the start: a world tour, a triple album, and matching gold jackets — all before their first paying gig.
Showy only wants attention — sequins and fireworks — while grandiose makes a claim about scale: the thing pretends to a grandeur its means cannot honor.
Delusional lies past grandiose: a grandiose plan is impractical but still recognizably a plan, while a delusional one has broken with reality altogether.

Overblown faults the telling: a review, a claim, or a reputation inflated past what the substance underneath supports. Grandiose faults the thing itself — plans, buildings, and promises whose scale has outrun their means. An overblown report of a modest success exaggerates; a grandiose plan was oversized from the start.

Puffed-up describes swelling past true size — an ego, a price, a title — and the swelling can be small and private. Grandiose needs real scale: schemes or structures pretending to a grandeur their means cannot honor. A puffed-up clerk brags; a grandiose one drafts plans for a marble headquarters.

In 1893, land promoter Elias Crane announced that the prairie town of Dry Creek -- population 312 -- would become 'the Chicago of the West.' His plans were grandiose even by the standards of a boom decade: a twelve-story opera house, a stock exchange, and a canal connecting the town to a river forty miles away.
Crane printed maps showing steamboats docking where, in fact, there was only buffalo grass.
The town's entire treasury could not have paid for one block of the opera house.
A few settlers bought lots.
Most read the numbers, looked at the dry creek bed, and kept their savings.
Work on the canal stopped after a hundred yards; the trench is still visible today, a scar recording the distance between Crane's vision and his means.
